did_you_know.text: Did you know? At the second banquet described in the chapter, King Ahasuerus and Haman come to drink with Queen Esther.
Did you know? The king again asks Esther what her petition and request are, promising that they will be granted and fulfilled—even up to half the kingdom.
Did you know? Esther distinguishes between two requests: “my life” in her petition and “my people” in her request—she asks for the rescue of both her life and the lives of her people.

Did you know? Esther emphasizes that the Jews had been sold to be destroyed, killed, and annihated; if they had merely been sold as male and female slaves, she says, she would not have troubled the king to the same extent.
Did you know? After Esther speaks, the king asks twice who the man responsible is: “Who is he, and where is he?”
Did you know? Esther does not merely name Haman; she calls him “a wicked enemy” and “this evil Haman.” At her words, Haman is terrified before the king and queen.
Did you know? The king goes out in anger into the palace garden, while Haman remains to plead with Esther for his life, realizing that disaster from the king is about to overtake him.

Did you know? When the king returns, he sees Haman falling on the couch where Esther is reclining and interprets it as an attempt to assault the queen in his own house; immediately, it is said that Haman’s face was covered.
Did you know? Harbona tells the king about a gallows fifty cubits high that Haman had prepared for Mordecai, who had spoken well of the king; the king orders Haman to be hanged on it.
Did you know? Haman is hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, and at the end of the chapter it is said that the king’s anger subsided.
